en: A nail stabs right into your car tire.
So why doesn't the tire go flat in seconds?
I'm Max, and this is Max Wise.
Let's look inside the tire.
Old car tires had two parts.
A tough outer tire, and inside it, a rubber balloon called an inner tube.
Poke a hole in that balloon, and the air rushes out fast.
It escapes around the tube and through the rim, so the tire can collapse quickly.
So engineers threw the tube away.
Now the tire itself holds the air.
That's a tubeless tire.
When a nail goes in, the rubber squeezes tight around it.
Air can only sneak out through that tiny gap, so it leaks slowly, and you have time to stop safely.
The seal starts at the bead.
A ring of steel wire at each edge sits in a groove in the wheel.
Air pressure pushes it outward, locking it in tighter and tighter.
Next is the skeleton.
Strong cords run across the tire from edge to edge, like the ribs of an umbrella.
They keep its shape at speed and steady in corners.
Then comes the tread, the only part that touches the road.
It needs the right balance of hardness, bounce and pattern to grip.
The hardest part is the rubber itself.
It must be soft enough to hug the road, but tough enough not to wear away.
So a nail in a tubeless tire usually means a slow leak, not a sudden blowout.
Don't pull it out yourself. Get it to a tire shop.
Stay curious!
